A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Hierarchical Successor Representation for Robust Transfer. Their main text, equations, figures, algorithms, and appendices are readable and support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original grid-world transfer experiments, representation analyses, and procedurally generated maze exploration results, including supplementary experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds experiments on online option construction, generalised policy improvement, alternative maze geometries, and option sensitivity.

M1.justification: v2 introduces online option construction in Appendix B.2 and Algorithm S2: agents begin without options, learn a primitive-action SR, construct eigenoptions after warm-up, and periodically refresh them while learning HSR. v1 assumed pre-acquired options and left iterative discovery to future work. This substantially extends the procedure while retaining the underlying HSR/NMF framework.

E1.justification: Transfer evaluation expands beyond the canonical four-room environment to an asymmetric four-room layout with barriers, a Loop maze, a Corridor maze, and a Multi-pairwise-bottleneck maze (v2 Figure S3). These test materially different environmental geometries and connectivity structures. The original transfer and procedural-maze exploration scenarios remain.

E2.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 5 add an actual SR-GPI comparison, evaluating policy composition with one-hot, HSR-row, and HSR-NMF representations against linear Q-learning. v1 discussed successor-feature research but did not evaluate this comparator family. The original representation and exploration baselines are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include withholding the target reward vector until first goal discovery before switching to GPI, testing agents without preconstructed options, and varying option budgets across 4, 8, 16, and 32. Figure S6 adds a 10,000-action coverage analysis; the retained main exploration figure still reports 100,000-action coverage. These are added protocols, not demonstrated reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands robustness analysis: Figure S3 tests dependence on environmental topology; Figure S4 compares eigenoptions, covering options, random target options, and option counts; Figure 2i-l and Figure S6 test transfer and exploration with online-discovered options. These address dependencies that v1's representation and offline-versus-online analyses did not test.

E5.justification: Mean ± standard error reporting and the 20-seed default remain, while several added experiments explicitly use 10 seeds. Figure S6 introduces two-way ANOVA interaction tests. Figure 5 describes a paired t-test but reports df = 18 for 10 seeds, leaving the exact test unclear. There is no evidence that retained experiments used fewer runs.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include online-option transfer benefits (Figure 2l, p = 0.026), no significant difference between one-hot SR-GPI and HSR-NMF Q-learning (Figure 5c, p = 0.199), and benefits from combining GPI with HSR-row/NMF (p = 0.003/0.007). New appendix results report robustness across geometries and stabilisation beyond eight options. These supplement largely unchanged original results.

T1.justification: v2 removes the leading discount factor from the main-text termination-kernel formula, matching v1's appendix expression. Appendix A changes the intra-option occupancy sum from ending at τ to τ−1, restores discounted continuation terms, explicitly conditions on termination states, and revises the contraction argument. These are mathematical revisions within the existing framework; Theorem 3.1's conclusion is retained.

C1.justification: The abstract's central transfer, representation, and exploration claims remain. However, the introduction now explicitly claims robustness to environmental geometry, option definition, and absence of preconstructed options. The discussion replaces v1's pre-exposure restriction with demonstrated operation using online option construction, materially broadening claimed applicability.

C2.justification: v2 interprets HSR representations and GPI policy composition as complementary, explains weak covering-option performance through restricted initiation sets and sparse rewards, and discusses stability beyond a modest option budget. It also qualifies online option construction as heuristic with unresolved theoretical foundations. These substantially extend interpretation and applicability boundaries while retaining the original topological explanation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository access statement, online-option initialisation and update pseudocode, and the reward-discovery implementation used for GPI comparisons. Existing transfer and exploration hyperparameters remain. Numerical warm-up and option-refresh intervals are not supplied, so the additional reproducibility documentation remains incomplete.

R1.justification: The relationship to successor-feature/GPI research is substantively revised: v1 emphasised its allegedly shared diffusion limitations, whereas v2 positions GPI as complementary algorithmic machinery and studies combinations with HSR. Carvalho et al. (2023) is added to this discussion, alongside new predictive-map connections citing Yu et al. (2020) and Piray and Daw (2021).

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain. v2 adds a GPI results subsection, organises Appendix B into subsections, inserts GPI implementation details, and locally rewrites related work and discussion. Typographical corrections, acknowledgements, and conference-header changes accompany these additions, without a wholesale language or structural rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from eight to twelve panels, and v2 adds a GPI schematic/comparison figure, topology and option-sensitivity figures, an online-exploration figure, and another algorithm display. These substantially expand the visual presentation. The original exploration Figure 5 becomes Figure 6, and the original spectral Figure S3 becomes Figure S5; neither is removed.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1: dependence on pre-acquired options, narrow transfer validation, and the absence of an evaluated GPI comparator. Online-option experiments and Figures S3-S6 substantially strengthen the empirical support, while the GPI comparison clarifies HSR's contribution relative to prior methods. The online procedure remains heuristic, some implementation settings are unspecified, and Figure 5's statistical reporting is inconsistent, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.
